alt: Higher earners pay a higher percentage of income in tax, and the state pays benefits to low-income groups. Examples are Brazil’s Bolsa Família (from 2003), conditional on school attendance and health checks, and India’s rural employment guarantee (2005). Other legal tools are a minimum wage, equal opportunities laws and measures such as job guarantees and quotas.
caption: Taxing higher earners more and paying benefits to the poor narrows the gap.

alt: A life line from cradle to grave. Free education supports childhood, unemployment benefits support working age and pensions support old age; free healthcare, low-cost housing and universal basic income, trialled in Finland in 2017–2018, apply throughout life. In Britain the Beveridge Report (1942) led to the NHS (1948).
caption: A welfare state protects life chances at every stage of life.

alt: Four kinds of NGO work: reducing poverty through cash transfers and food aid, medical assistance such as Médecins Sans Frontières, promoting business through microcredit (Grameen Bank), and improving education. BRAC combines all four. Criticisms: NGOs can create dependency, answer to donors, impose Western priorities and are too small to change structural causes.
caption: NGOs help directly, but critics say they cannot change structural causes.

alt: The welfare state sits between two critics. The New Right (Murray, 1984) say it does too much and creates an underclass. Marxists say it does too little, only softening capitalism. Below, Oscar Lewis’s culture of poverty, the idea of dependency culture, and feminist criticisms of equality laws, then an evaluation.
caption: The New Right say welfare does too much; Marxists say it does too little.

alt: A sending country and a receiving country. Push factors are poverty, unemployment, conflict, persecution and natural disasters; pull factors are jobs, higher wages, safety, education and family. Migrants move one way and remittances flow back. The sending country may suffer a brain drain; the receiving country gains workers, taxes and diversity, but migrants face stereotyping and racism.
caption: Show who gains and who loses on both sides of migration.

after: ## How do global ecological issues affect inequality? (3.3.2)
alt: Four cards. Transnational companies bring jobs and investment but may exploit cheap labour, weak regulation and resources. Climate change harms poorer countries most through drought, flooding and crop failure, though richer countries produced more emissions. Pollution from mining, factories and waste affects poor communities, and rapid urbanisation creates informal settlements.
caption: The costs of global production and climate change fall mostly on poorer societies.

alt: Arrows carry cheap labour, raw materials and profit from poorer to richer countries, the Marxist view of capitalist exploitation. Colonialism extracted resources and shaped economies around exports. Feminists add that women do much of the world’s work but own a small share of its property.
caption: Marxist, colonial and feminist explanations all show wealth moving away from the poor.
